title: Michigan’s last-gasp miracle by Bryce Underwood saves Whittingham debut from disaster
content:
ANN ARBOR, Mich. — A fraction of a second from a devastating loss, Michigan kicked off the Kyle Whittingham era with an improbable victory for the ages.

Quarterback Bryce Underwood connected on a 47-yard Hail Mary to JJ Buchanan to give No. 16 Michigan a 13-12 victory against Western Michigan, sending fans spilling out of the stands for an impromptu dance party Saturday night inside Michigan Stadium.

“We were flirting with disaster,” Whittingham said. “That would have been an epic loss. They’ll talk about this game for years, I’m sure.”

The play only happened because officials controversially ruled that Underwood’s first attempt at a Hail Mary sailed out of the end zone before time expired. Western Michigan players rushed the field in celebration, only to be sent back to the sideline after officials ruled that Michigan had 1 second remaining.

The Big Ten early Sunday morning released a statement and video footage explaining the call.

“Following video review, it was determined Western Michigan’s #18 started his jump from an established out-of-bounds position (left foot) and made contact with the ball with one second remaining on the clock. As shown in the provided video of what was viewed during the replay process, a side-by-side view of the play and the game clock, using a direct shot of the game clock in the stadium, was used to determine the final ruling.”

Whittingham said he thought time was remaining when he watched Underwood’s first Hail Mary in real time. Western Michigan coach Lance Taylor saw the opposite.

“When I looked up at the clock, it was past zeroes before we touched it,” Taylor said. “I knew they would review it. It was the last play of the game.”

NBC rules analyst Terry McAulay questioned the decision to put a second back on the clock on the TV broadcast, and Western Michigan president Russ Kavalhuna said the ending should be reviewed.

“We’ll talk to our commissioner, and we’ll try to see if there’s anything we can ask for a review on,” Kavalhuna said. “Frankly, I don’t know if we can. I just want everyone to know this football team deserves a second look if that’s possible.”

Underwood’s Hail Mary rescued Michigan from a nightmarish start in Whittingham’s first game as coach. After driving for a touchdown on their opening drive, the Wolverines didn’t score again until Buchanan snagged Underwood’s pass amid a crowd of defenders in the end zone.

Before Underwood dropped back to his final heave, Michigan seemed headed for certain defeat. The Wolverines looked out of sorts for most of the night, and Whittingham was visibly displeased with their performance.

Michigan had three turnovers, including a fumble by Underwood with 1:50 remaining when the Wolverines were trying to drive for a go-ahead field goal.

Western Michigan won the rushing battle and dominated time of possession, controlling the ball for more than 40 minutes.

“We know we’re not going to win a lot of ballgames this year if we don’t fix some things and fix them right away,” Whittingham said.

All the talk about Underwood’s offseason progress, his improved mechanics and consistency in camp, didn’t translate on the field. If anything, Underwood looked shakier than he did as a freshman starter last season.

Underwood went 12-of-22 passing for 170 yards and gifted Western Michigan 3 points at the end of the first half. His accuracy and decision-making were suspect once again. His best play for most of the night was a fumbled snap on Michigan’s opening drive that he recovered and threw to Buchanan, who made a one-handed grab of a high pass.

The interception at the end of the first half was inexcusable. Michigan was 80 yards from the end zone with 10 seconds remaining and hadn’t moved the ball at all since its first drive. Underwood threw an out route to the sideline that was intercepted and nearly returned for a touchdown. The play gave Western Michigan a field goal as time expired, and those 3 points loomed large as Western Michigan took a 9-7 lead in the fourth quarter.

Underwood wasn’t Michigan’s only problem, but his struggles were impossible to ignore. Michigan simply can’t win in the Big Ten without better quarterback play.

Offensive coordinator Jason Beck came to Michigan with a reputation for offensive turnarounds. This Michigan offense looked nothing like Beck’s offenses at Utah and New Mexico that finished No. 2 in the FBS in rushing.

If nothing else, Michigan appeared to have the personnel to run the ball effectively. That didn’t happen Saturday, as the Wolverines finished with 106 rushing yards on 25 carries, an average of 4.2 yards per rush.

Running back Jordan Marshall had just 44 yards on 11 carries, and five-star freshman Savion Hiter wasn’t a factor. Michigan’s offensive line, a unit that was expected to be a strength, generated little push against Western Michigan’s defensive front.

Aside from the opening drive, when Michigan cruised 75 yards for a touchdown, and the game-winning heave, the offense was moribund. Even when the Wolverines were lacking in offensive firepower last season, they knew they could run the ball. That wasn’t the case Saturday.

Only Michigan’s highly anticipated showdown against Oklahoma. But taking nothing away from Western Michigan, it’s hard to imagine the Wolverines having success against Oklahoma’s defense if they couldn’t move the ball against the Broncos.

The expectation for this season was that Michigan would be competitive against every team on the schedule, including Big Ten heavyweights Ohio State, Oregon and Indiana. Openers can be deceiving, and the Wolverines might not be as bad as they looked Saturday. There’s always the chance Saturday’s unlikely resurrection sparks a big step forward. While the celebration continues in Ann Arbor, there remain all sorts of uncomfortable questions for Whittingham, who was supposed to be the steady hand Michigan needed.
